sections.COMMENTS:
We propose that this Composite Source is located on a ramp of a major thrust of the Northern Apennines accretionary prism, emerging along the Adriatic coastline.
The geometry of this seismogenic area is constrained by seismic reflection profiles (Bally et al., 1986; Calamita et al., 1991, 1994; Barchi et al., 1998) and instrumental seismicity as no geological and geophysical seismogenic sources are contained within.
The activity of the northern Apennines thrust belt in a compressional regime, and particularly of its shallower and most frontal fronts, is still questioned having been proposed alternative tectonic frameworks (e.g.: Bertotti et al., 1997; Di Bucci and Mazzoli, 2002). In spite of this, recently released datasets of active stress data (e.g.: Vannucci and Gasperini, 2003; Montone et al., 2004), help defining the matter, clearly showing an active compression oriented perpendicular to the thrust fronts. For example the active stress map of Italy (Montone et al., 2004) shows in the Marche region a compressive tectonic regime, with Shmin directions rotating from E-W in the Po Plain to NW-SE along the Adriatic coast, following the trend of the main Apennines front.
The Umbria-Marche region was thoroughly investigated using seismic reflection profiles, and different interpretations of its structural style are available in the literature. The main differences in the interpretation of the structural style of this region are the position of the basal decollement level of the thrusting, and the presence or not of secondary decollement levels. Some researchers (Bally et al., 1986; Doglioni et al., 1994) indicate the bottom of the Triassic evaporites as the basal decollement level, and propose that a thin-skinned tectonic has characterized the Paleogene-Neogene evolution of the belt. Other researchers (Barchi et al., 1998; Finetti et al., 2001; Lavecchia et al., 2003) consider that also the upper portion of the magnetic basement was involved in thrusting, and propose a thick-shinned structural style. In general there is a good agreement among the researches (e.g., Coward et al., 1999; Barchi et al., 1998; Calamita et al., 1994) about the presence of two main decollement levels inside the accretionary prism, the lower coinciding with the bottom of the Triassic evaporites, on which the major thrust ramps originate, and the shallower coinciding with the Marne a Fucoidi or Scaglia Cinerea formation, on which minor thrusts sheet detach.
The deformation style of the Umbria-Marche region is characterized by two main structural levels: 1) a lower level consisting of deep and broad anticlines deforming the Mesozoic-Paleogene carbonate succession, produced by thrust faults detaching on the Triassic evaporites; and 2) a shallow level made up of small and tight anticlines, found in the axial zones of the major anticlines, and developed in the Neogene foredeep sediments. These last structures show a more complex structural pattern with respect the deeper ones.
Other geometrical features of this region are: 1) the occurrence of complex thrust trajectories, due to the presence of several potential detachment levels in the sedimentary multilayer; 2) decreasing upward wavelength of the anticlines; and 3) disharmony between different structural levels.
The Conero onshore area is presently affected only by low seismic activity, and was struck in historical time the 5.56 M 1269 Ancona and the M5.58 1690 Anconetano and earthquake (Rovida et al., 2016; CPTI15 catalogue). Furthermore, the area of the source is related with the 1972 M 4.2-4.7 seismic sequence (Rovida et al., 2016; CPRI15 catalogue).
The depth range of this Source is derived from seismological data from the eastern sector of the Northern Apennines, where shallow seismicity is registered. We suggest that this Source may be the easternmost and shallower portion of a leading thrust of the Apennine belt which activation in different time and at different depths produces damaging earthquakes along two parallel strips.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Are the Northern Apennines characterized by active subduction or is present deformation taken up by major lithospheric thrusts?
2) If subduction is active in the Northern Apennines, is the magnetic basement involved in thrusting? So, the structural style in this region is thin- or thick-skinned?
3) Is the Conero onshore seismogenic area a shallow segment of a major regional thrust? If so, is this thrust laterally continuous, and what is its length?
4) Is the Northern Apennines upper crustal seismicity related with the easternmost shallower seismicity found along the Adriatic coast line? And, does the shallower and deeper seismicity occur at different depth on the same thrust fault? And so, is the Conero onshore a shallow ramp of the same regional thrust, of which the Northern Apennines, Pesaro-Senigallia and Southern Marche seismogenic areas are deeper ramps?

pictures.t: Map of hypocenter distribution with depth
pictures.c: Map showing in the inner Marche region deep crustal seismicity with depth ranging between 14 and 35 km. Shallower seismicity associated with compressional events is recorded in the coastal and off-shore zones (from Chiarabba et al. [2005]).

Depth distribution of deep crustal and subcrustal earthquakes and geometry of the Adria lithosphere flexured beneath the Apennines. The lowermost profile cuts across the Marche region (from Chiarabba et al. [2005]).

pictures.t: Map of depth of seismogenic layer in Italy
pictures.c: A map of the depth of the bottom of the seismogenic layer in the Marche region shows progressively deeper earthquakes moving westward from the axis of the Northern Apennines. Shallower depths are again found along the Adriatic coastline (from Chiarabba et al. [2005]).

The Stress Map of Italy shows a NE-SW compressional tectonic regime acting in the coastal Marche region. The directions of Shmin follow the trend of the Northern Apennines fronts from the southern Marche to the Po Plain (from Montone et al. [2004], modified).

pictures.t: Profile of seismic activity in the Northern Marche
pictures.c: The profile highlights the earthquake activity of the central-northern Apennines along the Coastal Thrust Front (CTF) and the occurrence of a strip of deeper events to the southwest, possibly related to the deeper portion of the same thrust (from Burrato et al. [2004]).

pictures.t: Map and section of Sn attenuation zone in Italy
pictures.c: Map and cross-sections showing Sn attenuation zone in Italy. The cross-section perpendicular to the Northern Apennines suggests the presence of a westward dipping mantle slab in this area (from Mele et al. [1997]).

pictures.t: Map showing Moho depths along the CROP3 profile
pictures.c: Moho depths estimated along the CROP03 profile. The doubling of the Moho in the Val Tiberina and the westward deepening of the Adriatic Moho seen in the Marche region suggest the  existence of a slab of Adriatic lithosphere (from Mele and Sandvol [2003]).

pictures.t: Map and sections of converted seismic lines across the Marche coastline and offshore
pictures.c: Sections of two converted (time to depth) seismic lines in the Central Marche offshore. The sections were used to characterize the hypothesized source of the 1690 earthquake (original picture by S. Mariano).

pictures.t: Regional cross-sections across the Po Plain and the northern Adriatic Sea
pictures.c: Interpreted regional seismic reflection profiles straddling the full extents of the Adriatic basin, including the Po Plain and the adjacent Northern Apennines (to the west), Southern Alps (to the north), and Dinarides (to the east) (from Fantoni and Franciosi [2009]).
